A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AtomSurf, with matching authors, core architecture and Atom3d experiments. The supplied text, figures, tables and equations support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 adds readable Appendices A and B.

before.justification: v1 reports original surface and hybrid-model experiments on PIP, MSP and PSR, including quantitative comparisons, architectural ablations and qualitative predictions.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds binding-site classification results in Figure 3 and a DiffusionNet convergence comparison in Appendix B, Figure 5.

M1.justification: Section 2.3 introduces protein-scale-informed diffusion-time initialization using absolute samples from N(2,2). The core graph/surface architecture and residual bipartite GAT combination remain intact. Batching and BatchNorm were already described in v1 and are not new components.

E1.justification: v2 adds MaSIF-ligand binding-site classification, predicting one of seven co-factors from a binding site. This introduces a distinct ligand-preference task and dataset beyond the retained protein interaction, mutation stability and structure-ranking tasks.

E2.justification: MaSIF and HMR, previously cited without scored comparisons, become evaluated comparators in the new binding-site experiment, Figure 3. This adds direct comparisons against specialist surface-learning methods. The existing Atom3d comparator sets and adapted HoloProt baseline remain.

E3.justification: The binding-site experiment introduces 1,634/202/418 training/validation/test instances, balanced accuracy, chemical and geometric features comparable to the baselines, and parameter-count matching to HMR. Existing Atom3d splits and metrics remain unchanged. The reported surface-model depth changes from 'three or four' blocks to consistently three; this does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds a PSR validation-convergence comparison between original and modified DiffusionNet, testing the combined adaptations' optimization benefit. The existing architecture, message-passing and depth ablations, together with the PIP qualitative examples, are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or other uncertainty estimates. The new convergence curves and binding-site scores likewise provide no stated run aggregation or uncertainty.

E6.justification: Figure 3 newly reports binding-site balanced accuracy of 0.88 for AtomSurf, 0.81 for HMR and 0.74 for MaSIF; Figure 5 adds PSR convergence results. Existing tables also contain substantive revisions, including surface PSR local R from 0.32 to 0.330 and three-block attention PIP AuROC from 0.791 to 0.792. The principal Atom3d rankings remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v1 contains architectural equations but no scale proposition or proof. v2 introduces Proposition 2.1 on expected Brownian geodesic distance under uniform scaling, with an Appendix B derivation using eigenvalue, eigenfunction, heat-kernel and area scaling. This is substantive new mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The central claims that surface-only methods underperform and that graph/surface integration improves the tested Atom3d results remain. v2 extends the abstract and conclusion's state-of-the-art claim explicitly to ligand-binding pocket classification, without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds a substantial explanation attributing training instability to protein-scale variation, and explains hybrid design choices through complementary local/global processing and parameter allocation to message passing. v1 offered a briefer long-range-diffusion hypothesis. The conclusion also makes memory requirements an explicit limitation.

D1.justification: Sections 2.3–2.5 and Appendix A add task-specific depths and widths, encoder internals, BatchNorm placement, the 8-angstrom bipartite cutoff and implementation-library links. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to every disclosed setting. Conversely, v1's explicit Gaussian projection of atom features onto surface vertices is omitted; the project code/data link remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations on geometric GNNs, sequence models, over-smoothing and heat/surface geometry, including Duval, Rao, Li, Bronstein–Kokkinos, Meyer and Sun, while removing Méndez-Lucio et al. The central positioning around Atom3d, DiffusionNet and hybrid representations remains, with more specific discussion of graph-based limitations.

P1.justification: The introduction and methods are extensively rewritten. The original two method subsections become five, separating graph modeling, surface modeling, scale adaptation, hybrid representation and architecture. The conclusion is rewritten around conclusions and limitations, and implementation/proof appendices create a substantially different explanatory structure.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, redraws the representation overview and architecture schematic, and removes the separate v1 Figure 2 graph/surface illustration. It adds binding-site and convergence charts. Existing tables and qualitative predictions are resized or relocated, with the qualitative content preserved.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens weaknesses in v1's validation and reproducibility: Section 3.4 directly compares specialist surface methods under stated feature and parameter controls, while Appendix A supplies concrete architecture settings. The scale analysis and convergence evidence also make the adaptation rationale more assessable. These gains outweigh the omitted Gaussian-projection detail. Statistical uncertainty remains unreported, and the convergence comparison does not isolate individual modifications.
